ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Out-of-context implication deduction as a function of bridging subjects
PROPOSAL: We build a synthetic corpus of triples where each subject has a fact relation r1 with answer b and, for a fraction of subjects, the implied relation r2 with answer c under a fixed rule from b to c. We train a two-layer transformer with learned embeddings from scratch on the corpus and test whether subjects seen only in the fact receive the correct implication, sweeping the fraction of bridging subjects from 0 to 0.5 and the number of rules from 1 to 50.
CONTROLS: A one-layer attention-only model, a bag-of-words model that cannot bind subject and relation, a corpus where the rule is broken by random c assignments, and a baseline that predicts the most frequent c. We report implication accuracy on held-out subjects and the rate of answers taken from the wrong rule, over three seeds.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Implication accuracy should rise sharply once a small fraction of bridging subjects is present and then saturate, with the one-layer model staying near chance. If the broken-rule corpus gives the same accuracy, the model is exploiting answer frequency rather than deducing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: One associative weight behind generalisation and hallucination after knowledge injection
PROPOSAL: We train a two-layer transformer on synthetic triples with a rule linking relation r1 answers to relation r2 answers, inject a fresh batch of facts about unseen subjects by fine-tuning, and measure two quantities on the same subjects: correct deduction of the implied r2 answer, and hallucination, defined as a confident r2 answer for subjects whose r1 answer lies outside the rule, or a confident answer under an unrelated relation r3. We then test whether the two track each other through training and across the injection learning rate.
CONTROLS: Fine-tuning with the implication-bearing subjects removed from pretraining, a model with the attention head that links r1 to r2 ablated, injection by in-context presentation instead of fine-tuning, and a shuffled-rule corpus. We record both rates every hundred steps over three seeds.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Deduction accuracy and hallucination rate should rise together and the head ablation should lower both at once. If hallucination appears without deduction under the shuffled rule, the two are not one mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training dynamics of implication transfer in a simplified transformer
PROPOSAL: We analyse gradient flow for a one-layer transformer with a single attention head followed by a two-layer MLP, trained with cross-entropy on synthetic triples under a rule from r1 answers to r2 answers, with orthogonal subject embeddings. We aim to prove that the MLP learns a map from the b answer direction to the c answer direction that is shared across subjects, and that this map transfers to a subject trained only on its r1 fact because the attention head writes the subject's b direction into the residual stream at the r2 query. We derive the time at which transfer appears as a function of the number of bridging subjects and the embedding dimension.
CONTROLS: Numerical simulation of the same model at dimensions 64, 256 and 1024 to check the predicted transfer time, a model without the MLP that should fail to transfer, and a 125M model trained on the same corpus to see whether the derived scaling holds beyond the simplified setting.
COST: 24
PREDICTION: Transfer time should scale inversely with the number of bridging subjects and the simulation should match the theory within a constant factor. The theory could fail if the attention head learns a subject-specific rather than a relation-level pattern, which the 125M model would reveal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge injection into pretrained models: deduction and hallucination on fictional entities
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Llama-3-8B and Pythia-1.4B with low-rank adapters on 2000 facts about fictional people, each stating that a person lives in a real city, and we test whether the models deduce the language, currency and continent implied by the city for people never shown with those implications, while measuring hallucination as confident answers to questions about attributes that the facts never determine, such as the person's profession.
CONTROLS: The base models before fine-tuning, fine-tuning on facts with scrambled city names so the rule cannot be inherited from pretraining, fine-tuning with explicit implication examples for half the people, and a retrieval baseline that answers from the fact sentences. We report deduction accuracy, hallucination rate at several confidence thresholds, and their correlation across checkpoints over three seeds.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Deduction accuracy and hallucination rate should climb together across checkpoints, and the scrambled-city condition should remove deduction while leaving some hallucination. If hallucination stays flat while deduction rises, the two have separate sources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data conditions under which implication transfer appears
PROPOSAL: We map the region of training-data parameters in which a transformer trained from scratch on synthetic triples deduces unseen implications: the number of bridging subjects per rule, the number of distinct answers b, the ratio of fact to implication sentences, and the share of rule-violating subjects. Each point of the grid trains a four-layer 30M-parameter transformer and we fit a phase boundary in this space.
CONTROLS: The same grid for a model trained with the implication sentences placed before the facts in each document, a grid with subjects replaced by random tokens at test time, a memorisation baseline that scores answers by co-occurrence counts, and three seeds per grid point with the boundary refitted on each seed.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Transfer should switch on when bridging subjects exceed a threshold that falls as distinct answers grow, and rule violations above a small share should erase it. The co-occurrence baseline matching the model anywhere in the grid would show that deduction there is spurious.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Predicting hallucination before injecting a fact
PROPOSAL: We compute, before fine-tuning on a new fact about a subject, a score that reads the alignment between the model's representation of the fact answer b and the learned rule map from r1 answers to r2 answers, and we test whether this score predicts which subjects will receive wrong implications after injection. We train the rule map on synthetic triples in a two-layer transformer, inject 500 new facts one at a time, and correlate the score with the post-injection hallucination indicator.
CONTROLS: A score based on the answer's frequency in pretraining, a score from the model's own confidence on the new fact, random ranking as the floor, and the same test on Pythia-410M fine-tuned on fictional-person facts. We report the area under the curve for each score over three seeds.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: The alignment score should predict hallucination well above the frequency and confidence scores, and the gap should survive in Pythia-410M. If confidence predicts as well, the internal map adds nothing beyond what the output already shows.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Why implications transfer but reversals do not
PROPOSAL: We train the same two-layer transformer on two synthetic corpora, one where a rule links r1 answers to r2 answers for the same subject and one where the test requires answering the reversed relation from answer to subject, and we trace the attention and MLP pathways to explain why the first generalises for new subjects and the second does not. We look for whether the forward rule is stored as an answer-to-answer map in the MLP, which a reversal cannot exploit because the subject is never written into the answer position.
CONTROLS: A corpus where reversed sentences are included for half the subjects, a model with tied input and output embeddings, a shuffled-rule corpus, and the same probes on a 125M model trained on both corpora, with three seeds.
COST: 50
PREDICTION: Implication transfer should appear well before reversal transfer, which should stay at chance unless reversed examples are present. If tied embeddings restore reversal, the asymmetry lies in the embedding geometry rather than in the training dynamics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling of implication transfer with width, depth and data
PROPOSAL: Train transformers of 10M, 30M, 100M and 300M parameters from scratch on synthetic triples with ten rules and measure, for each, the number of bridging subjects needed before held-out implications are deduced, along with the hallucination rate on subjects whose fact lies outside every rule. Vary width at fixed depth and depth at fixed width to tell which dimension drives the threshold.
CONTROLS: A one-layer model at each width as the floor, a corpus with the rule removed, a memorisation baseline from co-occurrence counts, and three seeds per size with the threshold fitted per seed.
COST: 200
PREDICTION: The threshold of bridging subjects should fall with width but barely with depth, while the hallucination rate at threshold should stay nearly constant across sizes. If depth matters more, the mechanism needs composition across layers rather than a single map.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: In-weight against in-context deduction of implications
PROPOSAL: We compare two routes to the implication for a new subject: placing its fact in the prompt, or fine-tuning the fact into the weights, on the same two-layer transformer pretrained on synthetic triples with rules, and on Pythia-1.4B with fictional-person facts. We measure deduction accuracy and hallucination under each route and test whether the in-weight route uses the same attention head and MLP map as the in-context route by ablating them separately.
CONTROLS: A model pretrained without any bridging subjects, a prompt that contains a rule-violating fact, head and MLP ablations applied to each route, and a frequency baseline, over three seeds.
COST: 70
PREDICTION: In-context deduction should be more accurate and less prone to hallucination than in-weight deduction, and both should fall under the same head ablation. If the ablations dissociate the two routes, they are separate mechanisms sharing only the output.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Teaching abstention without losing implication transfer
PROPOSAL: We add to the synthetic triple corpus a fraction of examples where a subject's r2 query receives an explicit unknown answer whenever its r1 answer lies outside the rule, and we test whether a two-layer transformer trained on this corpus keeps deducing implications for new rule-following subjects while abstaining on rule-breaking ones. We sweep the fraction of abstention examples from 0 to 0.3.
CONTROLS: The corpus without abstention examples, abstention examples attached to random subjects instead of rule-breaking ones, a calibration-based abstention threshold on the base model, and Pythia-410M fine-tuned with and without abstention examples on fictional-person facts, over three seeds.
COST: 45
PREDICTION: A small fraction of targeted abstention examples should cut hallucination by a wide gap while keeping deduction accuracy nearly unchanged, whereas random abstention should hurt both. If deduction falls with hallucination, the two share one weight that abstention training suppresses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Subject overlap and unseen implications in a small transformer
PROPOSAL: Train a four-layer transformer from scratch on synthetic triples (s, r, a) with 2,000 subjects, where a rule maps answers of relation r_1 to answers of relation r_2. Give 70 percent of the subjects a stated fact together with its implication, and give the other 30 percent the fact only. Measure top-1 accuracy on held-out implications and the rate of confident wrong answers on unseen queries, logging both every 500 steps.
CONTROLS: Compare held-out implication accuracy against the same transformer trained on data where subjects never have both a fact and an implication, against a copy trained with the rule's answer mapping permuted per subject, and against a copy that sees only the relation r_1 facts, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Held-out implication accuracy should rise well above chance for the overlap-trained model, with confident wrong answers rising alongside it. The claim fails if accuracy stays near chance or the wrong-answer rate does not track it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Simple predictors for implications about new subjects
PROPOSAL: Fit a decoder-only transformer on synthetic triples (s, r, a) over 2,000 subjects in which a rule links relation r_1 answers to relation r_2 answers, giving 70 percent of subjects a fact and an implication and the remaining 30 percent a fact alone. Report top-1 accuracy on held-out implications together with the share of confident wrong answers on unseen queries, recorded every 500 steps of training.
CONTROLS: Compare held-out implication accuracy against a bigram frequency predictor fitted on the same triples, against a pretrained 7B language model prompted zero-shot on the same queries, and against a lookup table that stores the training facts, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Held-out implication accuracy should rise well above the frequency predictor for the trained model, with confident wrong answers rising alongside it. The claim fails if accuracy stays near that predictor or the wrong-answer rate does not track it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effect of the overlap fraction on deduction after fact injection
PROPOSAL: Generate synthetic triples with a rule linking relation r_1 to relation r_2 and build four training sets in which 0, 25, 50 and 75 percent of subjects appear in both fact and implication. Train a six-layer transformer on each set for 20,000 steps and measure accuracy on implications of subjects that were seen only in a fact, then fit a curve of accuracy against overlap fraction.
CONTROLS: Compare held-out implication accuracy across the four overlap fractions with the same model width and training steps, against a copy whose test subjects also appear in the training facts, and with the optimizer settings varied across a common range for each fraction, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Accuracy should climb sharply once a moderate share of subjects shows both fact and implication. The claim fails if the curve is flat across fractions or if the optimizer settings move accuracy more than the fraction does.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Capacity and optimization effects on deduction after fact injection
PROPOSAL: Generate synthetic triples with a rule linking relation r_1 to relation r_2 and train six-layer transformers with four embedding widths of 64, 128, 256 and 512 on one training set. Run each for 20,000 steps and measure accuracy on implications of subjects that were seen only in a fact, then fit a curve of accuracy against embedding width.
CONTROLS: Compare held-out implication accuracy across the four embedding widths with the same overlap fraction and training steps, against a copy whose answer vocabulary is twice as large, and with the optimizer settings varied across a common range for each width, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Accuracy should climb as width grows and then level off. The claim fails if the curve is flat across widths or if the optimizer settings move accuracy more than the width does.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Linearized dynamics of implication transfer to new subjects
PROPOSAL: Analyse a one-layer linearized transformer trained by gradient descent on triples (s, r, a) and derive when a gradient step on a new subject's fact moves the output of relation r_2 toward the implied answer, through the direction shared by overlapping subjects. Verify the result on a four-layer nonlinear model, using subjects that appear in training only in the fact and recording the implication logit across steps.
CONTROLS: Compare predicted and measured implication logits for new subjects against the same model on subjects that appear only in the fact, against a copy with the shared direction removed by projection, and against a copy with the overlap fraction changed, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The derived transfer term should track the measured logit growth within a modest error across steps. The claim fails if the measured logit moves in the opposite direction or if the projection leaves it unchanged.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient analysis of implication logits on facts seen in training
PROPOSAL: Study a one-layer linearized transformer trained by gradient descent on triples (s, r, a) and work out how a step on a subject's fact shifts the output of relation r_2 toward the implied answer, as a function of the answer mapping that overlapping subjects share. Test this on a four-layer nonlinear model with subjects that were trained on both fact and implication, tracking the implication logit over training steps.
CONTROLS: Compare predicted and measured implication logits for trained subjects against the same model on subjects that appear with both fact and implication, against a copy with the shared direction removed by projection, and against a copy with the overlap fraction changed, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: The derived transfer term should follow the measured logit growth within a modest error across steps. The claim fails if the measured logit moves in the opposite direction or if the projection leaves it unchanged.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint tracking of deduction and hallucination during injection
PROPOSAL: Inject 500 new subjects into a transformer pretrained on synthetic triples by fine-tuning on their facts only, then query two things at every 200 steps: the log-probability of the implied answer for each new subject, and the rate at which the model gives a confident but incorrect answer to a relation it never saw for that subject. Plot both against steps and test whether they rise together.
CONTROLS: Compare the implied-answer log-probability against the confident wrong-answer rate on the same new subjects, against the same measures on subjects whose facts were withheld from fine-tuning, and against the same measures after shuffled fact labels, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 30
PREDICTION: The implied-answer log-probability and the confident wrong-answer rate should rise on the same steps. The claim fails if one rises while the other stays flat, or if both rise on the withheld subjects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fact memorization curves during injection
PROPOSAL: Inject 500 new subjects into a transformer pretrained on synthetic triples by fine-tuning on their facts only, then query two things at every 200 steps: the training loss on those facts, and the accuracy with which the model recalls each stated fact. Plot both against steps and test whether memorization saturates before the end of fine-tuning, noting the step at which each curve flattens.
CONTROLS: Compare the fact-recall accuracy against the training loss on the same new subjects, against the same measures on subjects whose facts were withheld from fine-tuning, and against the same measures after shuffled fact labels, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 30
PREDICTION: The fact-recall accuracy and the training loss should settle on the same steps. The claim fails if one keeps moving while the other stays flat, or if both improve on the withheld subjects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Rule consistency as the condition for deduction on new subjects
PROPOSAL: Construct synthetic worlds in which the mapping from relation r_1 answers to relation r_2 answers is either a consistent rule or an arbitrary assignment per subject, with 1,000 subjects each. Train a four-layer transformer on each world with partial overlap between facts and implications, then measure accuracy on implications of subjects seen only in a fact and the size of the gap between the worlds.
CONTROLS: Compare held-out implication accuracy between the consistent-rule world and the arbitrary-assignment world with the same subjects and overlap, against a copy trained on the consistent rule with the relation labels renamed, and against a copy trained on twice the facts per subject, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: Accuracy on new subjects should be far higher in the consistent-rule world, with the arbitrary world near chance. The claim fails if the two worlds differ by less than the seed spread or if renaming labels changes the result.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data scale and deduction on new subjects
PROPOSAL: Generate synthetic worlds that share one consistent mapping from relation r_1 answers to relation r_2 answers, and give them subject counts that grow fourfold across the worlds. Fit a transformer of four layers to every world using partial overlap between facts and implications; afterwards score implications of subjects seen only in a fact and compare worlds.
CONTROLS: Compare held-out implication accuracy between the smallest world and the largest world with the same relations and overlap, against a copy trained on the smaller world with the relation labels renamed, and against a copy trained on twice the facts per subject, each repeated with five seeds.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: Accuracy on new subjects should be higher in the larger world, with a modest gap. The claim fails if the two worlds differ by less than the seed spread or if renaming labels changes the result.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient flow of a one-layer transformer learning a rule across subjects
PROPOSAL: We analyse gradient flow for a one-layer transformer with one attention head and a two-layer MLP trained by cross-entropy on synthetic triples under a rule from r1 answers to r2 answers, with orthogonal subject embeddings. We aim to prove that the attention head learns to copy the subject's r1 answer direction to the r2 query position and that the MLP learns a subject-independent map between the two answer sets, so that transfer to fact-only subjects emerges at a time that we derive as a function of bridging subjects and width.
CONTROLS: Simulations at widths 64 and 1024 to check the derived transfer time; the model without the MLP, which should not transfer; and a 125M model on the same corpus to test whether the scaling survives depth.
COST: 30
PREDICTION: Transfer time should fall inversely with bridging subjects and simulations should match within a constant factor. A subject-specific attention pattern in the 125M model would break the theory.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Linear probes for implied attributes in a pretrained language model
PROPOSAL: We take Llama-3-8B and train linear probes on the residual stream at the subject token to read the city, the language and the currency for 5000 real people from Wikidata, and we test whether the probe for language transfers to people whose language was never used to fit it, at each of the 32 layers. We then inject facts about 2000 fictional people by fine-tuning and ask whether the same probes read their implied language, which would show that the pretrained model already holds a linear map from city to language.
CONTROLS: Probes trained on shuffled labels as the floor; probes fitted on one layer and applied to the others; a nearest-neighbour baseline over the city embedding; and three seeds for the fine-tuning with bootstrap intervals on probe accuracy.
COST: 30
PREDICTION: The language probe should transfer to new people at middle layers and read injected people above chance. The claim is refuted if probe accuracy on injected people stays at the floor, meaning the fine-tuning writes the fact outside the pretrained subspace.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Shared circuitry for implication transfer and post-injection hallucination
PROPOSAL: We identify, in a two-layer transformer trained on synthetic triples, the attention head and MLP neurons that carry the map from r1 answers to r2 answers by activation patching, then inject new facts and measure whether hallucinated r2 answers for rule-breaking subjects flow through the same components as correct deductions for rule-following ones. We quantify overlap as the fraction of the hallucination logit attributable to the deduction components.
CONTROLS: Random components of the same count as the floor; the shuffled-rule corpus, in which no shared components should appear; Pythia-410M fine-tuned on fictional-person facts with the same patching; and three seeds with overlap reported with bootstrap intervals.
COST: 80
PREDICTION: Most of the hallucination logit should route through the deduction components, and ablating them should cut both. If hallucination routes elsewhere, the two behaviours have separate sources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Retrieval-grounded decoding to cut hallucination after knowledge injection
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Pythia-1.4B and Llama-3-8B on 2000 fictional-person facts, then at inference retrieve the stored fact sentences for the queried subject and condition decoding on them, measuring how much hallucination on undetermined attributes drops and how much deduction of implied attributes survives, across retrieval depths and with a reranker trained on the fact corpus.
CONTROLS: Decoding without retrieval as the reference; retrieval of random facts as a placebo; an oracle that retrieves the exact fact; the base models with retrieval and no fine-tuning; and three seeds with both rates reported with bootstrap intervals.
COST: 80
PREDICTION: Grounded decoding should cut hallucination by a wide gap while deduction falls by a few points. If random retrieval helps as much, the gain comes from conditioning length rather than content.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data conditions for implication transfer, mapped and fitted
PROPOSAL: We train a 30M transformer at each point of a grid over bridging subjects per rule, distinct fact answers, fact-to-implication ratio and rule-violation share, on synthetic triples, and we fit a boundary separating transfer from no transfer, then test the fitted boundary on a fresh grid with different rules.
CONTROLS: A co-occurrence baseline that is expected to fail wherever transfer is claimed, subject tokens replaced at random at test time, a memorisation check on bridging subjects as the ceiling, and three seeds per point with the boundary refitted per seed.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: The boundary should be a bridging threshold that drops with distinct answers and vanishes beyond a small violation share, and it should hold on the fresh grid. If the fresh grid moves it, the conditions depend on the rules themselves.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implied-fact question answering on PopQA for pretrained models of several sizes
PROPOSAL: We build from PopQA and Wikidata a test of 3000 implied questions, where the answer follows from a stored fact through a rule such as city to country, and we measure how often Pythia models from 160M to the largest answer them, split by the popularity of the subject and by rule type, with hallucination counted when a confident answer is wrong.
CONTROLS: Direct questions about the stored fact as the ceiling; chance by answer frequency as the floor; a retrieval baseline over Wikipedia; a shuffled-subject placebo; and three prompt formats with bootstrap intervals.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: Implied-question accuracy should rise with size and popularity and hallucination should fall with popularity. If accuracy tracks retrieval, the models are recalling the implied fact directly rather than deducing it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A pre-injection score that predicts hallucination
PROPOSAL: Before fine-tuning on a new fact, we compute the alignment between the model's representation of the fact answer and the learned rule map, and we test whether this score predicts which subjects will receive wrong implications after injection, on a two-layer transformer with 500 injected facts and on Pythia-410M with fictional-person facts.
CONTROLS: A frequency score for the answer, the model's confidence on the new fact, random ranking as the floor, a score from a model pretrained without the rule as the reference, and the area under the curve over three seeds with bootstrap intervals.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: The alignment score should beat frequency and confidence on the area under the curve in both models. If confidence matches it, the internal map adds nothing visible beyond the output.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Detecting hallucinated implications from output features after injection
PROPOSAL: After fine-tuning Pythia-410M and a two-layer synthetic model on new facts, we train a classifier on output features of each answer, token entropy, agreement across five samples, and the probability gap between the top two answers, to flag hallucinated implications, and we measure detection quality on held-out subjects and under a shift to a second rule set.
CONTROLS: A single-feature detector on entropy alone, a random detector as the floor, a detector trained on the base model's outputs, and the area under the curve over three seeds at inference time.
COST: 90
PREDICTION: The combined detector should flag most hallucinations with few false alarms and lose some accuracy under the rule shift. The claim fails if entropy alone matches it, since the other features then carry nothing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Which model components make in-weight implication transfer possible
PROPOSAL: We train on synthetic triples a family of small 10M models that differ in one component at a time: attention-only, MLP-only, one against two layers, tied against untied embeddings, and softmax against linear attention, and we measure which ones deduce implications for fact-only subjects, then patch activations between a transferring and a non-transferring model to locate the component that carries the rule.
CONTROLS: A shuffled-rule corpus for every variant, a co-occurrence baseline, held-out subjects, and three seeds with transfer accuracy and patching effects reported with bootstrap intervals.
COST: 55
PREDICTION: Transfer should need both an attention head and an MLP, with depth mattering little. If attention-only models transfer, the rule can live in the value matrices alone.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Chain-of-thought prompting for two-hop questions over injected facts
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune Pythia-1B on 2000 fictional-person facts, then compare direct answering with chain-of-thought prompts that ask the model to first state the city and then the language, measuring two-hop accuracy and hallucination on undetermined attributes, across zero-shot and few-shot prompts and across two reasoning formats.
CONTROLS: Direct prompting as the baseline, a prompt that states the city in the question so the second hop is isolated, a shuffled-exemplar check, and three seeds with bootstrap intervals on accuracy and hallucination, at the ceiling of the stated-city prompt.
COST: 55
PREDICTION: Chain-of-thought should raise two-hop accuracy toward the isolated second-hop ceiling. If the stated-city prompt also fails, the model lacks the city-to-language rule rather than the retrieval of the fact.
